content.overview: Indian administrative law rests on constitutional foundations: the rule of law, separation of powers (in a diluted form), fundamental rights (especially Articles 14, 19 and 21), and the judicial-review jurisdiction of the Supreme Court and High Courts.
content.glance: Identify the constitutional anchors (rule of law, fundamental rights, judicial review, Articles 323A/323B); apply them to the administrative action under challenge.
content.study: Unlike systems that developed administrative law primarily through ordinary legislation and common-law review, Indian administrative law is constitutionally entrenched. Article 14 supplies the non-arbitrariness standard; Articles 19 and 21 protect liberty and livelihood interests affected by administrative action; Articles 32 and 226 provide the writ jurisdiction that makes review effective; Articles 323A and 323B authorise tribunals subject to the basic-structure limits recognised in L. Chandra Kumar. Current-law framing: ground every administrative-law analysis in these constitutional provisions.

sections.heading: Rule of Law
sections.body: Public power must be authorised by law and exercised without arbitrariness.

sections.heading: Fundamental Rights
sections.body: Articles 14, 19 and 21 constrain administrative action affecting equality, freedoms and life/liberty.

sections.heading: Judicial Review
sections.body: Articles 32, 136, 226 and 227 secure the supervisory jurisdiction of constitutional courts.

sections.heading: Tribunals and Basic Structure
sections.body: Articles 323A/323B permit specialised adjudication subject to independence and residual High Court review.

sections.heading: Separation of Powers (Indian Adaptation)
sections.body: Indian constitutionalism accepts functional overlap but polices concentration of power and protects judicial independence.

examples.title: Arbitrary licensing refusal
examples.body: An authority refuses a licence without reasons or standards. Article 14 non-arbitrariness and judicial review under Article 226 supply the constitutional foundation for challenge.

examples.title: Tribunal ouster clause
examples.body: A statute excludes High Court review of tribunal decisions. L. Chandra Kumar and the basic-structure doctrine render the ouster ineffective.

hypotheticals.question: Can ordinary legislation override Article 14 constraints on administrative action?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Fundamental rights bind the State; administrative action inconsistent with Article 14 is unconstitutional.

hypotheticals.question: Is separation of powers rigid in India?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Indian constitutionalism accepts functional overlap while protecting core judicial and legislative functions.

distinctions.title: Constitutional foundations vs ordinary administrative rules

misconceptions.trap: Administrative law is independent of the Constitution.
misconceptions.correction: Indian administrative law is constitutionally anchored in fundamental rights and judicial review.

misconceptions.trap: Tribunal clauses can fully oust High Court review.
misconceptions.correction: High Court review under Articles 226/227 is part of the basic structure.

cases.name: L. Chandra Kumar v Union of India
cases.issue: Whether tribunal decisions can exclude High Court judicial review.
cases.ratioDecidendi: High Court judicial review under Articles 226/227 is part of the basic structure.
cases.holding: Tribunal model affirmed subject to constitutional supervision.
cases.relevance: Foundational authority on constitutional limits of tribunal design.

cases.name: Maneka Gandhi v Union of India
cases.issue: Content of procedure established by law under Article 21.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Procedure affecting life and liberty must be fair, just and reasonable.
cases.relevance: Constitutional foundation for fairness in administrative action affecting liberty.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should a constitutional-foundations problem be analysed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. Identify the administrative action. II. Map the applicable constitutional anchors (Arts 14/19/21/226/323A). III. Apply the relevant doctrine. IV. Conclude.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What should submissions contain?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Constitutional provisions engaged; administrative action identified; doctrine applied; precise relief under Art 226/32.

examTips: Link doctrine to the article that supports it.
Remember L. Chandra Kumar for tribunal review.

enhancement.definition: Indian administrative law is constitutionally founded on the rule of law, fundamental rights and judicial review.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Administrative power is subject to constitutional rights and residual judicial review that cannot be ousted.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: The Constitution supplies the supreme standards that administrative law enforces.
enhancement.problemApplication: Map action to constitutional provision; apply doctrine; state relief.
keyTakeaways: High Court review cannot be ousted.
